actions.justification: Mandatory first step. Patient has bradycardia (HR 55), hypotension (BP 95/60), and mild hypoxia (SpO2 95%) — continuous vital sign monitoring is essential for this hemodynamically compromised inferior STEMI patient.

Mandatory per AHA Class I guideline: 12-lead ECG must be obtained and interpreted within 10 minutes of first medical contact to confirm STEMI and identify inferior ST elevation. Also need right-sided leads (V4R) given inferior STEMI to assess RV involvement.
Mandatory assessment action to characterize onset, duration, quality, and radiation of chest pain for risk stratification and to guide reperfusion therapy timing decisions.
MANDATORY - Inferior STEMI confirmed. Door-to-balloon target <90 minutes. Immediate cath lab activation is required to minimize myocardial ischemia time.
MANDATORY - Aspirin 325mg chewable is Class I recommendation for all STEMI patients as antiplatelet therapy to reduce thrombus propagation.

MANDATORY - Dual antiplatelet therapy with a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or clopidogrel) is Class I for STEMI prior to PCI. Prasugrel should be used with caution given inferior STEMI with possible RV involvement.
MANDATORY action - Heparin or enoxaparin anticoagulation is required for STEMI management as adjunctive therapy before primary PCI. This is the only remaining mandatory action.

Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy for STEMI. Door-to-balloon target is <90 minutes; patient is already 30 minutes in. Cath lab has been activated - now formally arrange/confirm PCI to ensure timely reperfusion.
Patient SpO2 is 95%, which meets threshold for supplemental oxygen in STEMI. Supplemental oxygen is indicated to maintain adequate oxygenation during acute MI.

CRITICAL SAFETY: Patient has inferior STEMI with hypotension (BP 95/60) and bradycardia (HR 55), which are classic signs of RV infarction. Right-sided ECG (V4R) must be obtained BEFORE any nitrates to confirm/exclude RV involvement. Nitrates are absolutely contraindicated in RV infarction as they can cause severe hypotension.
IV access is essential for medication administration and fluid resuscitation. Patient is hypotensive (MAP 72, BP 95/60) and may require crystalloid bolus if RV infarction is confirmed.
High-sensitivity troponin should be obtained at presentation for baseline documentation of myocardial injury and to support diagnosis per AHA guidelines.

Patient has hypotension (BP 95/60) and bradycardia (HR 55) consistent with RV infarction in inferior STEMI. IV fluid challenge is indicated for RV infarction to maintain preload, as RV infarct patients are preload-dependent. Nitrates are contraindicated.

Cardiology consult is appropriate to guide management of inferior STEMI with suspected RV involvement and hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, bradycardia) while patient is being prepared for primary PCI.
Formal ECG interpretation including right-sided leads should be documented to confirm RV infarction, guide management decisions, and establish baseline for monitoring progression.

Patient has inferior STEMI with hypotension (BP 95/60, MAP 72) and bradycardia (HR 55), consistent with RV involvement. Right-sided ECG (V4R) already obtained. Volume loading with crystalloid is appropriate for RV infarction to maintain preload and support blood pressure. Nitrates are contraindicated.
Comparing with prior ECG can help characterize acuity and extent of ST changes, identify baseline conduction abnormalities, and guide ongoing management decisions while awaiting PCI.

Patient has inferior STEMI with HR 55 and BP 95/60. Beta blocker use requires caution given borderline hypotension and bradycardia, but if hemodynamics allow, beta blockers reduce myocardial oxygen demand and are guideline-recommended adjunctive therapy in STEMI. Clinical reassessment needed before administration given low HR and BP.
